summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module so SNMP can manage the Baseline Privacy Plus features of DOCSIS 1.1 and 2.0 cable modems and cable modem termination systems. Baseline Privacy Plus covers the security features of cable data service. This is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4131 defines a MIB module, a set of SNMP objects, for the security features of DOCSIS cable networks. It covers the keys a cable modem and the head-end system share, the certificates that identify them, the encryption of multicast traffic, and the checking of downloaded software images. The objects exist on both sides, so an operator can watch the state of the keys and ask the equipment to renew them.

questions: what is the docsis bpi+ mib
how to manage cable modem security with snmp
what encryption does docsis bpi+ use
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let operators monitor and manage the privacy and security features of DOCSIS cable modems.

tldr.problem: DOCSIS 1.1 and 2.0 cable modems and head-end systems run the Baseline Privacy Plus security suite, but there was no standard way to see or control that suite over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: The MIB module adds tables for authorization keys, traffic encryption keys, certificates, multicast encryption and authenticated software download, on both the cable modem and the head-end side, plus the objects that drive and report each of them.
tldr.outcome: An operator can now read the state of each key and certificate and can start re-keying when needed. The memo also warns that the traffic encryption keys use 40-bit or 56-bit DES. RFC 4131 was later updated by RFC 9141.

today: RFC 4131 was published in September 2005 as a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9141. The memo's own warning about DES in the traffic encryption keys still stands as written.

sections.title: The Internet-Standard Management Framework
sections.content:
For a detailed overview of the documents that describe the current Internet-Standard Management Framework, the memo points to section 7 of RFC 3410.

Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, termed the Management Information Base or MIB. MIB objects are generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms defined in the Structure of Management Information (SMI). This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant to SMIv2, which is described in STD 58, RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is a named set of counters and settings a device exposes. SNMP reads and writes them, and SMIv2 is the notation this document uses to define them.

sections.title: The Four Areas of Baseline Privacy Plus
sections.content:
This MIB module, the BPI+ MIB, provides a set of objects required for the management of the Baseline Privacy Interface Plus features of DOCSIS 1.1 and DOCSIS 2.0 Cable Modem and Cable Modem Termination System. The specification is derived from the operational model described in the DOCSIS Baseline Privacy Plus Interface Specification.

DOCSIS Baseline Privacy Plus is composed of four distinct functional and manageable areas: key exchange and data encryption, cable modem authentication, multicast encryption, and authentication of downloaded software images.

The BPI+ MIB module is an extension of the DOCSIS 1.0 Baseline Privacy MIB module defined in RFC 3083, which is derived from the operational model described in the DOCSIS Baseline Privacy Interface Specification. The original Baseline Privacy MIB structure has mostly been preserved in the Baseline Privacy Plus MIB. The referenced DOCSIS specifications only require that Cable Modems process IPv4 customer traffic, and design choices in this MIB module reflect those requirements. Future versions of the DOCSIS specifications are expected to require support for IPv6 as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Baseline Privacy Plus does four things for a cable network: agree keys and encrypt traffic, prove which modems are allowed on the network, encrypt multicast traffic, and check that downloaded software is genuine. This document gives each of those a set of manageable objects.

sections.title: Structure of the MIB
sections.content:
The MIB module is structured into several tables and objects.

On the cable modem side, the docsBpi2CmBaseTable contains authorization key exchange information for one CM MAC interface, and the docsBpi2CmTEKTable contains traffic key exchange and data encryption information for a particular security association ID of the cable modem. Multicast encryption information is maintained under docsBpi2CmMulticastObjects, where there is currently one multicast table object, docsBpi2CmIpMulticastMapTable, that manages IP multicast encryption. Digital certificates used for cable modem authentication are accessible via docsBpi2CmDeviceCertTable, and cryptographic suite capabilities for a CM MAC are maintained in the docsBpi2CmCryptoSuiteTable.

On the cable modem termination system side, the docsBpi2CmtsBaseTable contains default settings and summary counters for the system, the docsBpi2CmtsAuthTable contains Authorization Key Exchange information for each CM MAC interface as well as data from CM certificates used in cable modem authentication, and the docsBpi2CmtsTEKTable contains traffic key exchange and data encryption information for a particular security association ID. Multicast encryption information is maintained under docsBpi2CmtsMulticastObjects, which holds two multicast table objects: docsBpi2CmtsIpMulticastMapTable, designed specifically for IP multicast encryption, and docsBpi2CmtsMulticastAuthTable, meant to manage all multicast security associations.

The docsBpi2CmtsIpMulticastMapTable defines the object docsBpi2CmtsIpMulticastMask, which could be a non-contiguous netmask. This is why the object syntax is based on the InetAddress textual convention of the INET-ADDRESS-MIB module instead of InetAddressPrefixLength. It is to facilitate the assignment of the same DOCSIS Security Association ID to one or more IPv6 multicast group IDs matching one or more IPv6 multicast scope types within an entry in this table.

The docsBpi2CmtsCertObjects group contains two manageable tables, one for provisioned cable modem certificates and one for certification authority certificates. The docsBpi2CodeDownloadControl objects manage the authenticated software download process for a given device.
sections.plainLanguage: The module mirrors the equipment. On the modem side there are tables for the keys, the certificates and the multicast mapping; on the head-end side there are the matching tables plus the defaults the head-end applies to every modem.

sections.title: BPI+ and the Original BPI MIB
sections.content:
The BPI+ protocol interface is an enhancement to the BPI protocol, and it is a distinct protocol from BPI. The associated BPI+ managed objects should be considered separate from the BPI MIB objects defined in RFC 3083.

DOCSIS 1.1 and 2.0 systems implement both the BPI+ and BPI protocols to be backward compatible with 1.0 systems. For more information regarding the interoperability between BPI and BPI+ compliant systems, the memo refers the reader to appendix C of the DOCSIS BPI+ specification. For MIB module requirements it points to section 4.6.1 and figure 9 of the DOCSIS 1.1 OSSI specification, and to section 7.6.1 and tables 7 to 9 of the DOCSIS 2.0 OSSI specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Baseline Privacy Plus is a different protocol from the older Baseline Privacy, so its objects are kept apart from the older ones. Modern equipment runs both so that older modems still work.

sections.title: Relationship with the Interfaces Group MIB
sections.content:
The BPI+ MIB module is the management framework of the Baseline Privacy Plus Interface Specification, which provides the MAC layer security services of DOCSIS through the Baseline Privacy Key Management protocol. The BPI+ MIB module objects are organized as extensions of the Radio Frequency Interface Management module defined in RFC 2670.

The MIB table structures of this module are extensions of the DOCSIS CATV MAC layer interface. In particular, the provisions of the Interface Group MIB defined in RFC 2863 for counter discontinuities and system re-initialization apply to the cable modem and the termination system, so that the difference between two consecutive counter polls can be validated.

All BPI+ MIB module counters are 32 bits, based on the minimum time to wrap up considerations of RFC 2863 and their possible frequency of occurrence as BPI+ finite state machine event counters.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects hang off the usual interface rows, so an operator polls them the same way it polls interface counters. The counters are 32 bits wide and follow the same rules about wrapping as other interface counters.

sections.title: The Managed Objects
sections.content:
The definitions in section 3 run from the module identity docsBpi2MIB down through the tables listed above. A few of the objects show what the module actually carries.

In docsBpi2CmBaseTable, docsBpi2CmPrivacyEnable says whether the modem is allowed to run without data encryption, docsBpi2CmPublicKey holds the modem's public key as an octet string of up to 524 octets, and docsBpi2CmAuthState reports the state of the cable modem authorization finite state machine, with the values start, authWait, authorized, reauthWait, authRejectWait and silent. The table also holds the key sequence number, the times at which the current and next authorization keys expire, the grace times, and the wait timeouts, each in seconds.

The docsBpi2CmTEKTable describes the attributes of each cable modem Traffic Encryption Key association. The modem maintains no more than one TEK association per security association ID per CM MAC interface, and the modem must create one entry per SAID regardless of whether the SAID came from a Registration Response message, from an Authorization Reply message, or from any dynamic SAID establishment mechanism. Each entry carries the encryption and authentication algorithms, the TEK state, the sequence number, the expiry times and counters for key requests, replies, rejects and invalids.

On the termination system side, the docsBpi2CmtsBaseTable holds the defaults the head-end applies, such as docsBpi2CmtsDefaultAuthLifetime and docsBpi2CmtsDefaultTEKLifetime in seconds, together with docsBpi2CmtsDefaultSelfSignedManufCertTrust and docsBpi2CmtsCheckCertValidityPeriods, and a set of summary counters for authentications, rejections and SAID mapping requests.

The docsBpi2CodeDownloadControl group covers the authenticated software download process. docsBpi2CodeDownloadStatusCode reports the result of the latest config file CVC verification, SNMP CVC verification or code file verification, using the values configFileCvcVerified, configFileCvcRejected, snmpCvcVerified, snmpCvcRejected, codeFileVerified, codeFileRejected and other. The group also holds the manufacturer's organization name and the code access start and CVC access start times.
sections.plainLanguage: The modem's own table says whether it is authorized, which key it is on and when that key runs out. The head-end table holds the lifetime defaults and the counters. The download group reports whether the software file passed its signature check.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A number of management objects in this module have a read-write or read-create MAX-ACCESS and may be considered sensitive. The memo lists the ones where a malicious SET could cause a denial of service or a theft of service, or compromise the intended data privacy of users. The re-key objects docsBpi2CmAuthReset, docsBpi2CmtsAuthCmReset and docsBpi2CmtsTEKReset are used for initiating a re-key process, so a massive SET attack may cause CMTS processing overload and compromise the service. The lifetime objects docsBpi2CmtsDefaultAuthLifetime, docsBpi2CmtsDefaultTEKLifetime, docsBpi2CmtsAuthCmLifetime and docsBpi2CmtsTEKLifetime control how long keys last, and implementers are encouraged to follow the range constraints defined in the compliance clause. Changing the multicast objects can remove customers or multicast groups, causing service disruption, and can also constitute theft of service by authorizing non-subscribed users to multicast groups.

Readable objects are sensitive too. If the information in the base, TEK, authentication and certificate tables is accessible, attackers may use it to distinguish users configured to work without data encryption and to learn the current Baseline Privacy parameters in the network. It is therefore important to control even GET and NOTIFY access to these objects and possibly to encrypt their values when sending them over the network via SNMP.

SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. It is RECOMMENDED that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, including full support for the SNMPv3 cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The memo then turns to the encryption itself. The Baseline Privacy Plus Traffic Encryption Keys use 40-bit or 56-bit DES in CBC mode, and there is currently no mechanism or algorithm defined for data integrity. Because of the weaknesses in DES, future revisions of the DOCSIS BPI+ specification should introduce more advanced encryption algorithms and should also adopt authentication algorithms. The memo notes that frequent key changes do not necessarily reduce the risk of a DES attack, because traffic encryption keys, which are configured per cable modem and per BPI+ multicast group, can be used to decrypt old traffic even when they are no longer in active use. The cable modem authorization protocol uses triple DES encryption, which offers improved robustness in comparison with DES for CM authorization and TEK re-key management.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing to these tables can break the network, and reading them can tell an attacker which modems are unprotected. The memo also says plainly that the traffic keys use DES, which is weak, and that changing keys often does not fix that because old keys still decrypt old traffic.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The MIB module in this document uses the IANA-assigned OBJECT IDENTIFIER value recorded in the SMI Numbers registry, docsBpi2MIB { mib-2 126 }.
sections.plainLanguage: The module is registered under the number 126 in the SMI Numbers registry.

viz.caption: THE FOUR AREAS OF BASELINE PRIVACY PLUS

items.title: Key exchange and data encryption
items.text: The authorization key and the traffic encryption keys.

items.title: Cable modem authentication
items.text: Proving a modem is allowed on the network, using certificates.

items.title: Multicast encryption
items.text: Encrypting multicast traffic and mapping groups to security associations.

items.title: Software image authentication
items.text: Checking that a downloaded configuration or code file is genuine.

viz.caption: THE TABLES IN THE BPI+ MIB

items.label: start
items.desc: The authorization state machine is in its initial state.

items.label: authWait
items.desc: Waiting for the authorization exchange to complete.

items.label: authRejectWait
items.desc: Waiting after an authorization request was rejected.

items.label: silent
items.desc: The modem is not sending traffic.

items.label: configFileCvcVerified
items.desc: The configuration file passed its CVC verification.
